title: The Maharaja at the Akal Takht
hook: tradition says the Nihang leader Akali Phula Singh summoned Ranjit Singh to the Akal Takht for penance and he came humbly

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nalwa, the general who held the frontier even as he died; your line was the frontier held. Today, a summons.

A message arrives at the palace in Lahore. It isn't from a rival king or the British. It comes from the Akal Takht at Amritsar, addressed to the Maharaja himself, and it says, in effect: you have broken Sikh discipline; come and answer for it. The man who sent it has no kingdom. He leads a band of Nihangs, fierce, plain-living Sikh warriors. The man receiving it rules the Punjab. Everyone at court waits to see what he'll do.
screen: `A SUMMONS FROM AMRITSAR.` → `ADDRESSED TO THE MAHARAJA.` → `SENT BY A MAN WITH NO KINGDOM.`

segments.voice: First, the place. The Akal Takht, the throne of the Timeless One, faces the Harmandir across the walkway at Amritsar. Sikh tradition says Guru Hargobind raised it as the seat where the community's worldly affairs would be decided before God. From there, the Khalsa can call any Sikh to account. Any Sikh. Next, the man. Akali Phula Singh was a Nihang leader known for courage and strictness, and tradition remembers him serving at the Akal Takht. He fought in Ranjit Singh's campaigns. But when, as the story goes, the Maharaja's own conduct broke Sikh discipline, Phula Singh did not look away. He summoned him. Then the moment. Tradition says Ranjit Singh came, not with soldiers, but on foot, with folded hands. He admitted the wrong and accepted the punishment given, by the common telling a flogging, and bared his back. The gathered Sikhs, seeing the ruler of the Punjab with his head bowed, were so moved that they cried out for mercy, and the punishment was set aside for a fine. Notice who's above whom. In the Sarkar-e-Khalsa, the king spoke of serving the Khalsa. Here, for one morning, it wasn't just a phrase. In the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak says that sweetness and humility are the essence of every virtue. The Maharaja who laughed about his one eye could also bow his head.
screen: `THE THRONE OF THE TIMELESS.` · `PHULA SINGH SENDS A SUMMONS.` · `ON FOOT, WITH FOLDED HANDS.` · `THE SANGAT CRIES FOR MERCY.` · then, large: `EVEN THE KING BOWED.`

segments.voice: Think of a time someone told you that you'd got something wrong, and they were right, and let the memory come without flinching. Picture receiving it again, hands open and head a little lowered, not crushed, just willing, and notice what loosens when you stop defending; Waheguru on each breath out, if you pray.
Akal Takht, the throne of the Timeless One at Amritsar, where Akali Phula Singh summoned the Maharaja, who came humbly and accepted the Khalsa's correction. Today's word.
Your line: even the king bowed. Sweetness and humility, says Guru Nanak. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sikhs regard the Akal Takht in Amritsar as the seat from which the Khalsa can call any Sikh to account, and the story of Ranjit Singh accepting Akali Phula Singh's summons is told as an example that no Sikh stands above it.
